analysis.one_liner: Requires factories in smoggy areas to renew air permits every five years under tighter pollution limits.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a House vote: introduced in March 1989 with one cosponsor, it sat in the Energy and Commerce Committee and its health subcommittee until the Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required that permits for new large factories and other stationary air pollution sources in areas that fail federal air quality standards expire after five years. When a permit was renewed, the source would have had to keep all its existing pollution conditions and meet the "lowest achievable emission rate" as of the renewal date — so its allowed pollution would tighten over time instead of staying fixed for the life of the plant. The bill was referred to a House committee and died without a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live and breathe in "nonattainment areas" — communities that fail federal air quality standards, often heavily industrialized cities and their downwind neighborhoods. With the bill in place, each five-year permit renewal would have forced major new pollution sources in those areas to install the cleanest available technology of the moment, gradually cutting smog and toxic emissions around the plants.

how_it_helps.text: It ends permanent pollution deals: permits for new major sources in nonattainment areas could last no more than five years, so communities would no longer be locked into a plant's original emission levels for its entire life.

At each renewal, the plant would have to meet the lowest achievable emission rate determined at that time, meaning air quality would improve as cleaner technology becomes available rather than staying frozen at whatever the plant installed when it opened.
Renewed permits could not be weaker than the expiring permit — the source had to keep at least as stringent conditions — so the ratchet only moved toward cleaner air.

analysis.who_pays: Owners and operators of new major industrial sources — refineries, power plants, factories, and similar facilities — in nonattainment areas, which would face repeated capital upgrades to the best available pollution controls every five years, and potentially higher consumer prices for their products as a result.

drawbacks.text: The bill placed the entire burden on new and renewing industrial sources in nonattainment areas, forcing recurring capital investments in control technology every five years with no phase-in or relief, which industry would predictably oppose as costly and unpredictable.

Because it required compliance with the lowest achievable emission rate 'determined at the time of reissuance,' the standard could ratchet up repeatedly over a plant's life, and the bill offered no mechanism to help small operators absorb those costs.
It applied only to new sources permitted under the nonattainment permit program, so existing plants' emissions — often the largest share of a dirty air district's pollution — were untouched.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health benefit for people living near major pollution sources in smoggy areas was real and structural: a five-year renewal cycle with a moving technology standard would have steadily ratcheted emissions down. The cost fell on a narrow, well-defined group — operators of new industrial plants in nonattainment areas — in the form of periodic control upgrades. That trade-off (slightly costlier compliance, cleaner air for neighbors) is the standard design of nonattainment permitting, and the bill used it more aggressively than baseline law. Its real weakness was scope: it only reached new and renewing sources, leaving existing plant emissions alone.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its health subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote until the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Esteban Torres of California introduced the bill on March 22, 1989, joined by one cosponsor, Representative Henry Waxman of California.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, the committee that controls clean air legislation.
On April 24, 1989, the committee referred it further to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment — the standard last stop for a bill a committee has no plans to move.
No further action was ever taken; the bill was never reported out of subcommittee, and it died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Operators of new industrial pollution sources in nonattainment areas were better off, because they never had to face a five-year renewal cycle that would force them to upgrade to the best available pollution controls on a repeating schedule. Residents of smoggy communities got nothing.

for.name: Rep. Esteban Edward Torres
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill; his Los Angeles-area district sat in one of the nation's worst nonattainment regions

for.name: Rep. Henry Waxman
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as its only cosponsor

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: John Dingell, D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and never reported it out; the bill also died in its Subcommittee on Health and the Environment with no hearing or markup

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so the partisan shape can only be guessed from sponsorship: two House Democrats behind the bill and no Republican cosponsors.

industries.industry: Industrial air emitters (refineries, power plants, factories) in nonattainment areas
industries.note: The bill would have forced these plants to renew their permits every five years and install the best pollution controls available at each renewal, converting a one-time compliance cost into a recurring one. Their interest in avoiding that schedule ran directly against the interest of nearby residents in cleaner air.

A rolling five-year requirement to meet the lowest achievable emission rate would have created recurring demand for scrubbers, filters, and other control technology as standards tightened at each renewal.
